{"input": {"clarifying_context": "Customers: Enterprise platform admin teams adopting RHOAI MaaS for governed AI model access — large financial services, healthcare, and tech companies running OpenShift AI at scale (e.g., major banks using Azure OpenAI through MaaS governance, Fortune 500 companies standardizing on RHOAI for multi-provider LLM access)
Business justification: This is a MaaS GA completeness requirement. The 3.4 release already supports external model registration via CLI and surfaces them in AAE, but the lack of UI creates an admin experience gap that undermines MaaS adoption. Enterprise customers expect full dashboard management for governed model endpoints — CLI-only registration is a barrier to platform admin productivity and discoverability.
User problem: Platform admins must use kubectl/CLI to register external models into MaaS — there is no dashboard discoverability of which external providers are configured, no way to update or remove registrations from the UI, and AI engineers cannot easily distinguish configured external MaaS models from other endpoint types. This is fundamentally different from Custom Endpoints (which are unmanaged, ad-hoc connections without subscription binding or admin governance). MaaS external model registration requires admin ownership, MaaS subscription inclusion, and credential management at the MaaSModelRef level — all of which currently require CLI.
Scope: Single focused need — adding UI support for external MaaS model registration CRUD operations on the Model Deployments page. Form must capture provider (dropdown: OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex AI), endpoint URL, model name/identifier, and credential reference. MVP providers are OpenAI, Anthropic, and Bedrock; stretch goal includes all supported providers. Dependency on STRAT-102 (External Model Egress via IGW) backend landing first. CLI path must continue to work — this is additive UI, not a replacement.
Success criteria: Platform admin can create a new external MaaS model registration from the dashboard with provider selection, endpoint URL, model identifier, and credential reference; registered external model appears in AAE for AI engineers with correct MaaS subscription access; platform admin can view, edit, and delete existing external MaaS model registrations from the dashboard; UX is reviewed and approved by design team before implementation.", "priority": "Critical", "prompt": "Right now in RHOAI 3.4, platform admins can only register external model endpoints (like OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex AI) as MaaS-governed models through the CLI by creating MaaSModelRef CRDs. There's no dashboard UI for this at all. We need to add the ability to register, view, edit, and delete external model endpoint registrations directly from the Model Deployments page in the RHOAI dashboard. **Assessing the decision not to revise:**

The RFE scored 9/10 with individual dimension scores of: what: 2/2, why: 1/2, open_to_how: 2/2, not_a_task: 2/2, right_sized: 2/2. The only dimension not at maximum is "why" at 1/2.

The reviewer notes: "To strengthen for future reference: include named customer accounts experiencing this friction (e.g., 'XYZ Bank's admin team cited CLI-only registration as a barrier to MaaS adoption') or quantified business impact."

**Should the pipeline have attempted to revise to improve the "why" score?**

The "why" dimension at 1/2 represents a gap where concrete customer evidence is missing. However, this is the kind of information (named accounts, specific revenue figures, deal risks) that cannot be fabricated or inferred by an automated pipeline — it requires real customer data. An auto-revision attempting to strengthen "why" would either hallucinate customer names/numbers or produce generic filler that doesn't actually improve the score. The pipeline correctly recognized that:

1. The RFE is already at a high score (9/10) and passes the threshold.
2. The one weak dimension (why) requires real-world business intelligence that cannot be auto-generated.
3. The recommendation is "submit" — the RFE is ready as-is.

The feasibility review is thorough and well-reasoned, identifying genuine strategy considerations (credential management UX gap, design approval timing, provider-specific validation, AAE discovery verification) without conflating them with blockers. The review provides actionable feedback without being prescriptive.

The RFE itself is well-structured with clear problem statement, acceptance criteria, scope definition, and open questions. It appropriately separates what from how — describing the UI capability needed without prescribing implementation details.
